title: Validate Binary Search Tree
statement: Given the root of a binary tree, decide whether it is a valid binary search tree: every node's left subtree holds only smaller keys and its right subtree only larger keys.

nearMiss.why: Level order doesn't carry the min/max bounds each node inherits from all its ancestors.
You aren't searching for a key; you're checking an ordering property across the whole tree.
An explicit stack can drive an iterative inorder walk, but the idea is still a DFS that checks bounds (or inorder order).

trigger.answer: every node's left subtree holds only smaller keys
wrong: Given the root of a binary tree
trigger.why: A property that must hold for whole subtrees ⇒ recursive DFS passing (min, max) bounds down (or an inorder walk that must be increasing).

ds.answer: Recursion with Long (or nullable Integer) lower and upper bounds
wrong: int bounds initialised to Integer.MIN_VALUE / MAX_VALUE
ds.why: int bounds break when a node actually holds Integer.MIN_VALUE or MAX_VALUE.

invariant.answer: valid(node, lo, hi) checks that every key in node's subtree lies strictly between lo and hi.
wrong: Each node only needs to be compared with its direct children.
The left child is always exactly one less than its parent.
Bounds are reset at every level.
invariant.why: Going left tightens hi to node.val; going right tightens lo.

space.why: Recursion depth; O(n) for a skewed tree.

wrong: BFS only works on balanced trees.
BFS would need the keys sorted first.

approach: valid(node, lo, hi): null ⇒ true; if node.val ≤ lo or ≥ hi ⇒ false; return valid(left, lo, node.val) && valid(right, node.val, hi).

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
statement: Given a binary tree (not a search tree) and two nodes p and q in it, return their lowest common ancestor: the deepest node that has both p and q as descendants (a node counts as its own descendant).

nearMiss.why: The BST trick (go left if both are smaller) needs ordered keys; this tree is not a search tree.
BFS with parent pointers works but needs O(n) maps; post-order DFS answers it directly.
Tarjan's offline LCA uses DSU for many queries; one query only needs one DFS.

wrong: a node counts as its own descendant
trigger.why: Answer depends on what each subtree contains ⇒ post-order DFS that bubbles up 'found p/q'.

ds.answer: Recursion returning a TreeNode (p, q, the LCA, or null)
wrong: HashMap<TreeNode, TreeNode> parent map with a HashSet of ancestors
int[] Euler tour with a sparse table
ds.why: The parent-map approach works but uses O(n) extra; the recursive return value is enough.

invariant.answer: lca(node) returns p or q if found in that subtree, the LCA if both are found, else null.
wrong: lca(node) returns the depth of node.
lca returns true only when node equals p.
invariant.why: The first node where both sides return non-null is the LCA.

wrong: Binary search can't run on trees.
Binary search would return the deepest node.
Binary search needs p and q to be leaves.

approach: If node is null, p or q, return node. left = lca(node.left), right = lca(node.right). Both non-null ⇒ node; else return the non-null one.

twists.change: You are given the two nodes with parent pointers, but not the root.
twists.statement: Each tree node has a parent pointer. Given two nodes p and q (the root is not given), return their lowest common ancestor.
twists.ds: HashSet<Node> of p's ancestors (or two pointers that switch starts)

nearMiss.why: The recursive LCA search starts at the root, which you don't have.
There's no root to start a level order from.
There are no merges; the parent chain is already given.

twists.why: Two upward paths meet at the LCA ⇒ the 'intersection of two linked lists' problem: a visited set, or two pointers that restart at the other node.
twists.approach: Walk up from p adding to a set; walk up from q until a node is in the set. (O(1) space: a = p, b = q; a = a.parent ?? q, b = b.parent ?? p until equal.)

title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
statement: A path in a binary tree is any sequence of connected nodes (it need not pass through the root, and each node appears at most once). Node values may be negative. Return the maximum sum of any path.

nearMiss.why: Kadane's 'extend or restart' idea appears inside, but on a tree you must combine left and right subtrees with DFS.
Level order can't combine the best downward paths of both children.
There's no linear index; the subproblems are subtrees.

trigger.answer: need not pass through the root
wrong: each node appears at most once
trigger.why: Best path can bend at any node ⇒ DFS returns the best downward gain while a field tracks the best path through each node.

ds.answer: Recursion returning an int gain, plus a field (or int[1]) for the global best
wrong: int[n] dp indexed by node id
ds.why: What the parent can use (one branch) differs from the answer (both branches).

invariant.answer: gain(node) = node.val + max(0, gain(left), gain(right)); best is updated with node.val + max(0, gain(left)) + max(0, gain(right)).
wrong: best only considers paths starting at the root.
invariant.why: A parent can extend only one branch; a bend uses both.

wrong: Kadane only works on positive numbers.
Kadane needs the tree to be balanced.
Kadane can't be applied to integers.

approach: gain(node): if null 0; l = max(0, gain(left)); r = max(0, gain(right)); best = max(best, node.val + l + r); return node.val + max(l, r).

title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
statement: Given the root of a binary tree, return its node values level by level, from left to right within each level.

nearMiss.why: DFS with a depth index can fill per-level lists, but BFS gives level order naturally.
A stack is LIFO; level order needs FIFO.
Same BFS idea, but a tree needs no visited set and the point here is grouping by level.

trigger.why: Per-level output ⇒ queue BFS, snapshotting queue.size() for each level.

wrong: ArrayDeque<TreeNode> used as a stack (push / pop)
ds.why: FIFO order keeps levels in order.

invariant.answer: At the start of each outer loop, the queue holds exactly one full level, left to right.
wrong: The queue always holds all nodes seen so far.
The queue is sorted by value.
Each level is processed by popping until the queue is empty.
invariant.why: Processing exactly size nodes empties that level and enqueues the next.

time.why: Each node enqueued and dequeued once.

space.why: The queue holds one level at a time (plus the output).

approach: Queue the root. While non-empty: size = queue.size(); poll size nodes into a list, enqueue their children; add the list.

title: Binary Tree Right Side View
statement: Imagine standing on the right side of a binary tree. Return the values of the nodes you can see, ordered from top to bottom.

nearMiss.why: Following only right pointers misses levels where the rightmost node is in a left subtree.
A plain stack walk doesn't group nodes by depth.
No next-greater relationship is involved.

trigger.why: One answer per level (the last node of each level) ⇒ level-order BFS. (DFS visiting right-first and recording the first node at each depth also works.)

ds.answer: ArrayDeque<TreeNode> queue, recording the last node of each level
ds.why: Level snapshots identify the rightmost node directly.

invariant.answer: When processing a level of size s, the s-th node polled is the rightmost node at that depth.
wrong: The rightmost node is always a right child.
The root's right child is visible at every level.
Each level has at most two nodes.
invariant.why: BFS processes each level left to right.

time.why: Every node is visited (the visible one may be deep in a left subtree).

wrong: Linked lists can't store tree values.
Linked-list traversal needs the tree balanced.

approach: BFS by level; append the last node polled in each level. Or DFS(node, depth) visiting right before left, adding node when depth == result.size().

title: Binary Tree Vertical Order Traversal
statement: Return the vertical order traversal of a binary tree's values: column by column from left to right, and within a column from top to bottom (left before right when two nodes share a row and column).

nearMiss.why: Plain DFS visits deeper left nodes before shallower right ones, breaking top-to-bottom order unless you also track and sort by row.
Bucketing by column is part of it, but the order within a column comes from BFS.
Sorting everything with a heap by (col, row) works in O(n log n), but BFS gives the order for free.

trigger.answer: within a column from top to bottom
wrong: column by column from left to right
trigger.why: Top-to-bottom order within each column ⇒ BFS carrying a column index; bucket by column.

ds.answer: ArrayDeque of (node, column) pairs + HashMap<Integer, List<Integer>> column → values with min/max column tracked
ds.why: Tracking min and max column avoids sorting keys; a TreeMap also works at O(log n) per insert.

invariant.answer: Nodes are dequeued in row order (and left before right within a row), so appending to column lists keeps each column top to bottom.
wrong: Columns are processed one at a time.
Each column holds exactly one node.
The root is always column 0 and leaves are column −1.
invariant.why: Root column 0; left child column − 1; right child column + 1.

time.why: BFS plus O(1) map operations; no sort with min/max tracking.

wrong: DFS only works for complete trees.
DFS needs a heap to visit nodes.

approach: BFS with (node, col). Append node.val to map[col]; enqueue (left, col − 1), (right, col + 1). Output map from minCol to maxCol.

title: Diameter of Binary Tree
statement: Return the length (in edges) of the longest path between any two nodes of a binary tree. The path does not have to pass through the root.

nearMiss.why: Level order gives depths per level, but the longest path bends at some node: you need left and right heights at every node, bottom-up.
Two BFS passes (farthest node, then farthest from it) work on general trees, but recursion on a binary tree is simpler.
There's no array of states; the 'DP' is the post-order return value.

trigger.answer: does not have to pass through the root
wrong: longest path between any two nodes
trigger.why: Best path can bend at any node ⇒ post-order DFS returning height, updating a global best with left + right.

ds.answer: Recursion returning height, plus an int field (or int[1]) for the best diameter

invariant.answer: height(node) = 1 + max(height(left), height(right)); at each node the longest path bending there is height(left) + height(right).
wrong: The diameter always includes the root.
The diameter equals the tree's height × 2.
Leaves have height 1 and contribute 1 edge.
invariant.why: With null → 0, left + right counts edges.

time.why: Each node once (calling height() at every node from the top would be O(n²)).

wrong: BFS only works on balanced trees.
BFS would count nodes instead of edges, which is wrong by one.

approach: int height(n): if null return 0; l = height(n.left); r = height(n.right); best = max(best, l + r); return 1 + max(l, r).

title: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
statement: Design two functions: one turns a binary tree into a string and the other rebuilds exactly the same tree (same shape and values) from that string. Any encoding is allowed.

nearMiss.why: It is two methods on a class, but there's no combination of structures: one traversal order with null markers is the whole trick.
An explicit stack can drive an iterative pre-order, but the idea is the traversal with null markers, not stack matching.
Hashing values loses structure; duplicates and shape can't be rebuilt from a map.

wrong: turns a binary tree into a string
trigger.why: One traversal (pre-order) that also records nulls is enough to rebuild a unique tree recursively.

ds.answer: StringBuilder for pre-order with "#" for null; on decode, an Iterator<String> / ArrayDeque<String> of tokens consumed recursively
ds.why: In-order alone is ambiguous; heap indexing blows up on skewed trees.

invariant.answer: The decoder consumes tokens in exactly the order the encoder wrote them: node, then its whole left subtree, then its whole right subtree; '#' closes a branch.
wrong: Each level is written on its own line.
Values must be unique for decoding to work.
The string length equals the number of nodes.
invariant.why: Null markers make the pre-order sequence unambiguous.

time.why: Each node (and null) once each way.

wrong: A design approach would need a database.
Design classes must store the tree in a HashMap.

approach: serialize: pre-order, append val or '#', comma-separated. deserialize: split into a queue; build(): t = poll; if '#' return null; node = new TreeNode(t); node.left = build(); node.right = build().

title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
statement: Given the preorder and inorder traversal arrays of a binary tree with unique values, rebuild and return the tree.

nearMiss.why: Neither array is level order; the recursion follows pre-order.
The inorder array isn't sorted (it's a binary tree, not a BST), so you look the root up in a map instead.
An iterative stack solution exists, but the recognisable shape is recursive split: root, left range, right range.

trigger.why: Pre-order gives the next root; its inorder position splits left and right subtrees ⇒ recursive divide.

ds.answer: HashMap<Integer, Integer> value → inorder index, plus a pre-order cursor and recursion on index ranges
ds.why: The map makes each split O(1); copying subarrays makes it O(n²).

invariant.answer: build(lo, hi) consumes the next pre-order value as the root of the inorder range [lo, hi]; everything left of it in inorder is its left subtree.
wrong: The root is the middle of the inorder array.
Pre-order and inorder have the root at the same index.
Left subtrees are built after right subtrees.
invariant.why: Build left before right so the pre-order cursor stays in sync.

time.why: Each node is created once with an O(1) lookup.

wrong: BFS needs a sorted inorder array.
BFS would build the mirror image.

approach: Map inorder value → index. pre = 0. build(lo, hi): if lo > hi null; root = preorder[pre++]; m = idx[root]; root.left = build(lo, m − 1); root.right = build(m + 1, hi).

title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
statement: Given the root of a binary search tree and an integer k, return the k-th smallest value among its nodes (1-indexed).

nearMiss.why: A size-k heap over all nodes ignores the BST order, which already yields sorted values via in-order traversal.
Level order doesn't visit values in sorted order.
Without subtree sizes stored, you can't decide left/right by rank; in-order counting is the direct way.

trigger.why: BST + 'k-th smallest' ⇒ in-order traversal visits values ascending; stop at the k-th.

ds.answer: Iterative in-order with ArrayDeque<TreeNode> as a stack (or recursion with a counter)
wrong: ArrayList<Integer> of all values, then sort

invariant.answer: In-order visits nodes in ascending order, so the counter equals the rank of the current node.
wrong: The leftmost leaf is always the k-th smallest.
The root is always the median.
The counter equals the node's depth.
invariant.why: Follow-up with frequent updates: store subtree sizes.

time.why: Descend to the minimum, then k steps.

space.why: The stack holds one root-to-node path.

wrong: A heap can't store tree values.
A heap would give the k-th largest.

approach: Push lefts from root; pop node, if −−k == 0 return node.val; go to node.right and push its lefts.

title: Binary Tree Zigzag Level Order Traversal
statement: Return the values of a binary tree level by level, alternating direction: the first level left to right, the next right to left, and so on.

nearMiss.why: DFS with a depth index can fill per-level lists, but you'd still insert at the front on odd levels; BFS gives levels naturally.
Two stacks can produce zigzag order, but the underlying shape is still level-by-level traversal.
There's no grid to walk; the 'zigzag' is only the output order per level.

wrong: the first level left to right
trigger.why: Per-level output ⇒ BFS with level size; alternate by adding to the front or back of each level's list.

ds.answer: ArrayDeque<TreeNode> queue plus a LinkedList<Integer> / ArrayDeque<Integer> per level (addFirst or addLast)
ds.why: Children are queued in normal order; only the output list flips.

invariant.answer: At the start of each round the queue holds exactly the next level; leftToRight decides where each value goes in that level's list.
wrong: The queue alternates children order each level.
The queue holds two levels at once.
Values are sorted within each level.

space.answer: O(w) for the widest level (O(n) worst case)

wrong: DFS would visit levels in reverse order only.

approach: BFS by level size; for each node add val to the level list's back if leftToRight else front; enqueue children left then right; flip.

title: Minimum Depth of Binary Tree
statement: Return the number of nodes on the shortest path from the root of a binary tree down to the nearest leaf (a node with no children).

nearMiss.why: It is BFS, but on a tree: no visited set, no grid, just levels.
There is a single source, the root.
All edges have weight 1, so plain BFS already finds the shortest path.

trigger.why: Nearest = shortest unweighted distance ⇒ BFS, returning at the first leaf reached (DFS must explore every branch).

ds.answer: ArrayDeque<TreeNode> queue processed level by level
ds.why: Naive min(left, right) + 1 returns 1 for a node with a single child.

invariant.answer: Levels are processed in increasing depth, so the first leaf dequeued is at minimum depth.
wrong: The leftmost leaf is always the nearest.
The queue only ever holds leaves.
Depth increases with every node dequeued.
invariant.why: BFS can stop early, which DFS cannot.

time.answer: O(n) worst case, often much less

space.answer: O(w) for the widest level reached

wrong: Graph traversal can't be used on trees.
Graph BFS would need edge weights.
Graph traversal only works on grids.

approach: depth = 1; BFS by level; if a node has no children return depth; after each level depth++.
